claims.text: Enhancing short-range chemical order in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys produces a stronger magnetocaloric response at low applied fields.
Improved local chemical order increases the uniformity of magnetic exchange interactions.
Improved local chemical order increases the strength of magnetic exchange interactions.
More uniform and stronger magnetic exchange interactions sharpen the magnetic phase transition.
Magnetic behavior is coupled to lattice and structural energetics in rare-earth-free 3d-transition-metal high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced spin-lattice coupling minimizes magnetic hysteresis.
Enhanced short-range order provides well-connected metallic bonding pathways that support rapid heat transfer.
A high-entropy-stabilized matrix preserves mechanical stability during the proposed ordering treatment.
Controlled thermal annealing can increase short-range chemical order without causing phase separation or precipitation.
The experimental baseline is a homogeneous, single-phase, rare-earth-free high-entropy alloy with a relatively random atomic distribution.
Relative to the unannealed baseline, annealed samples with more short-range order should have a higher low-field magnetocaloric entropy change.
Relative to the unannealed baseline, annealed samples should have narrower magnetic hysteresis loops.
Relative to the unannealed baseline, annealed samples should have improved thermal conductivity.
Relative to the unannealed baseline, annealed samples should have improved mechanical stability.
The hypothesized behavior is restricted to a compositional and annealing window that retains a single phase.
Annealing conditions that induce phase separation or precipitation fall outside the hypothesis's domain.
A graded annealing series, with short-range order and magnetic, thermal, and mechanical properties measured against an unannealed control, can test the hypothesis.
Failure of increased short-range order to improve low-field magnetocaloric response and reduce hysteresis while maintaining thermal conductivity and mechanical stability would falsify the hypothesis.
